historical_timeline.summary: Born in Los Toldos, Province of Buenos Aires.
Fainted; appendectomy. Weakness and anemia from vaginal bleeding followed.
Advanced cervical cancer found; treated with radium.
Hysterectomy for cancer that had spread to adjacent pelvic organs; she was not told the diagnosis.
Recurrence confirmed without telling her; more radiotherapy, later chemotherapy.
Reported prefrontal lobotomy in the last months of her illness (contested reconstruction).
Barron Lerner's account of her illness published in The Lancet.

claims.statement: She was born Eva María Ibarguren on May 7, 1919, in Los Toldos, a village in the Province of Buenos Aires, Argentina; her marriage contract later gave her birth date as May 7, 1922.
She married Juan Perón on October 22, 1945, and became Argentina's first lady after his election in 1946. Her work for the poor made her a powerful political figure, and she is best known as Evita.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Identity only; her public work anchors the modern social history.

source_links.locator: married Juan Perón on October 22, 1945; first lady after the 1946 election
efforts for the poor made a powerful political figure; Evita

claims.statement: Her medical ordeal began in January 1950, when she was 30: she fainted and underwent an appendectomy. Despite persistent weakness and anemia from vaginal bleeding, she delayed further tests.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern presenting problem (abnormal bleeding with anemia). Reported from the medical historian Barron Lerner's research; no medical record was fetched.

source_links.locator: the cancer made its presence felt in 1950

claims.statement: In August 1951, much weaker, she developed increasingly severe abdominal pain and fainted again. Examination showed advanced cancer of the cervix, and Argentine doctors treated her with radium, then a standard therapy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only. The modern diagnosis and treatment are synthetic.

source_links.locator: her husband was told in September 1951 that she had an advanced cancer of the uterus

claims.statement: In October 1951 the New York cancer surgeon George Pack examined her under anesthesia to confirm the cancer, and in November 1951 he performed extensive surgery, a hysterectomy, because the cancer had spread to adjacent pelvic organs. He entered the operating room after she was anesthetized and left before she awoke. She underwent both procedures believing she had vague female problems, and was not told she had cancer; the secrecy kept the diagnosis from her and from the public during a presidential campaign.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only. The concealment is the teaching contrast for the modern episode, in which the diagnosis is told to her first and fully.

claims.statement: When abdominal pain returned in February 1952, her doctors confirmed, again without telling her, that the cancer had recurred. It shrank for a time with more radiotherapy, but the pain returned in May 1952, and chemotherapy failed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only.

claims.statement: She died on July 26, 1952, at 33, never knowing that she had cervical cancer.

source_links.locator: died on July 26, never knowing that she had cervical cancer

claims.statement: A study by Nijensohn and colleagues, published online in 2011, reported evidence that she underwent a prefrontal lobotomy in Buenos Aires in the last months of her illness, for pain, anxiety and agitation from metastatic cancer; the evidence includes a neurosurgeon's memoirs and press interviews, accounts of people close to her, and skull radiographs. A later paper by the same author argued that the operation was also meant to change her behavior.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, without detail; a retrospective reconstruction from indirect evidence, not a medical record. Not carried into the modern episode.

claims.statement: The medical historian Barron Lerner, who reported the case in The Lancet in 2000, said it showed how far medical practice and ethics have changed: patients with cancer were then rarely told what they had, whereas most patients in the United States are now told their diagnosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An interpretation of the concealment; the reason the modern episode documents truthful, culturally sensitive disclosure to the patient herself.

claims.statement: The Pap smear, which can find cervical cancer at its earliest stage, was developed in 1942, but in 1950 it was not yet standard medical care in the United States or Argentina.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context for the modern screening history, which is synthetic (never screened).

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and gynecologic oncology for a 31-year-old Spanish-speaking woman who has never had cervical screening and presents with abnormal bleeding and anemia: a speculum examination, direct biopsy of a visible cervical lesion with HPV testing and cytology, truthful and culturally sensitive disclosure of the diagnosis to the patient herself first, in her own language, with her choosing who else is told (the teaching contrast with the concealment of her historical diagnosis), FIGO 2018 staging with pelvic MRI and PET-CT, definitive chemoradiation with weekly cisplatin and image-guided brachytherapy for stage IIB disease, fertility and ovarian function counseling before treatment, management of anemia, treatment side effects and radiation-induced menopause, psychosocial support, and survivorship care, on the NCCN cervical cancer guideline, the FIGO 2018 staging system, the ASCCP 2019 management guidelines, the ASCO guidelines on patient-clinician communication, fertility preservation, and anxiety and depression, and the CMID anemia monograph.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient with four months of bleeding after intercourse and between periods and tiredness: history in Spanish, speculum examination, a visible cervical mass biopsied, HPV test and cytology, anemia tests, and her wishes about how results are given

Staging results (pelvic MRI and PET-CT), FIGO stage, and her treatment and fertility decisions before chemoradiation
Same-day sick visit for burning on passing urine during chemoradiation
Review two weeks after completing chemoradiation and brachytherapy: side effects, menopause symptoms, and survivorship care
Review three months after treatment: PET-CT response, examination, anemia, mood, and the follow-up plan
Periodic adult preventive visit after cancer treatment

hpi.narrative: Ms. Perón returns eight days after her first visit, as arranged, to hear her biopsy result in person; the visit is in Spanish. Before giving the result, Dr. Barragán asked what she understood so far and how she wanted to hear news. She said she suspected something serious, wanted to know everything, directly and herself, and wanted no one else in the room. She was told plainly that the biopsy shows a cancer of the cervix, an invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and that the HPV test found HPV type 16 and the cytology also showed cancer cells. After a pause and some tears she asked whether it can be cured, whether she will be able to work, and whether she could have children. Dr. Osei-Bonsu of gynecologic oncology then joined, with a professional Spanish interpreter, as Ms. Perón agreed. referral.question: A friable, exophytic cervical mass about 4 cm across in a 31-year-old woman who has never had cervical screening, with four months of bleeding after intercourse and between periods and iron deficiency anemia. A punch biopsy, HPV test and cytology were taken today. Please see her on the day the biopsy result is given, to confirm the diagnosis, stage the disease, advise on treatment by stage, and counsel her about fertility and ovarian function, and help us give her the result as she has asked
referral.urgency: Urgent, within one to two weeks, on the day of her biopsy result
referral.pertinent_history: Four months of bleeding after intercourse and between periods, with heavier periods, tiredness, breathlessness on stairs, and a dull pelvic ache. Never had cervical screening; no HPV vaccine; one male partner; no pregnancies. Never smoked. Speculum examination: a friable exophytic mass about 4 cm across on the cervix that bleeds on contact; bimanual examination limited by tenderness; no inguinal nodes. Urine pregnancy test negative. Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, mean cell volume 72 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL, white cells 7.1 and platelets 398 x10^3/uL: iron deficiency anemia from blood loss; ferrous sulfate started. Pelvic pain 4 of 10; acetaminophen, not anti-inflammatory painkillers. PHQ-2 1. Spanish is her preferred language for health care; please book a professional medical interpreter, not a family member. She asked that all results be given to her first, in person, and that she alone decide what her family and colleagues are told
questions: If the biopsy confirms cancer, what is its type, and what is its FIGO 2018 stage, and which imaging is needed to stage it?

How should her bleeding, pain and anemia be managed before and during treatment?
Will you help us give her the diagnosis directly, in Spanish, in the way she has asked, and plan how information is shared with her from here on?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Perón, a 31-year-old foundation director, is seen at the request of Dr. Barragán on the day she was told her biopsy result. The consultation is in Spanish through a professional medical interpreter, at her wish. She has had four months of bleeding after intercourse and between periods, with heavier periods, tiredness and a pelvic ache. She has never had cervical screening and was not vaccinated against HPV. She has no children and has not been pregnant. Dr. Barragán gave her the diagnosis in Spanish earlier in this visit; she has heard it, asked whether it can be cured, whether she can keep working, and whether she could have children, and asked that I explain the next steps to her directly
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Barragán's intake note. Cervical punch biopsy: invasive squamous cell carcinoma. HPV test positive for HPV 16; cytology with squamous cancer cells. Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, ferritin 6 ng/mL. Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, eGFR 117 today. PHQ-9 9 and GAD-7 9 today

exam.finding: With her consent and a chaperone: a friable exophytic tumor about 4.5 cm across replacing the cervix; colposcopy of the vagina shows no spread to the vaginal walls; on rectovaginal examination the left parametrium is thickened and nodular but does not reach the pelvic wall; the right parametrium and the rectal mucosa are free

assessment.display: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
assessment.assessment: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix related to HPV 16, about 4.5 cm with clinical spread into the left parametrium: at least FIGO 2018 stage IIB on examination. FIGO 2018 allows imaging to assign stage: a pelvic MRI defines local extent and an FDG PET-CT looks for nodal and distant spread, which would change the radiation fields and the stage. With parametrial spread, radical hysterectomy is not advised; the standard treatment, with intent to cure, is pelvic external beam radiation with weekly cisplatin, followed by image-guided brachytherapy, completed within eight weeks, because a longer overall time lowers the chance of cure. Kidney function allows cisplatin. HIV testing is recommended at diagnosis. Chemoradiation will end her ability to carry a pregnancy and will very likely end ovarian function; egg or embryo freezing needs about two weeks of stimulation and would delay treatment slightly, and laparoscopic ovarian transposition can sometimes preserve hormone function; any later pregnancy would need a gestational carrier. The decision is hers. Bleeding is now light; if it becomes heavy, vaginal packing or a few early radiation fractions control it. Anemia should be corrected before radiation with iron, and hemoglobin watched weekly during it. Acetaminophen is the right analgesic; anti-inflammatory painkillers should be avoided with cisplatin. The diagnosis was given to her first, in her language, and she asked to hear everything; I explained the plan to her directly and answered each of her questions honestly
From chronic tumor bleeding; oral iron is reasonable now that the bleeding is lighter, with transfusion only if hemoglobin falls sharply or she has symptoms

recommendations: Pelvic MRI and FDG PET-CT within ten days to assign the FIGO 2018 stage
HIV and hepatitis C tests now

If staging confirms stage IIB without nodal or distant spread: pelvic external beam radiation 45 Gy in 25 fractions with cisplatin 40 mg/m2 weekly, then image-guided high-dose-rate brachytherapy, all within eight weeks
Before treatment, her decision about egg or embryo freezing (reproductive endocrinology within days if she wants it) or ovarian transposition; treatment should not be delayed beyond about two weeks
Continue ferrous sulfate and acetaminophen; no anti-inflammatory painkillers during cisplatin; weekly blood count, creatinine and magnesium during treatment
Oncology social worker from today; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at diagnosis, before treatment, mid-treatment and after
All discussions with her directly, in Spanish with a professional interpreter when the clinician does not speak Spanish; information shared only with the people she chooses
After treatment: PET-CT at about three months, a vaginal dilator, and hormone therapy if ovarian failure occurs
